p.src: About a week later, I happened to hear a curious story from Chuck, the doctor. It was said that a ghost had begun appearing in Tock's house. By then the female kappa had gone off somewhere else, and the home of our poet friend had been converted into a photographer's studio. According to Chuck, whenever a photograph was taken in this studio, Tock's figure would invariably appear, before anyone knew it, as a dim shape behind the sitter. Chuck, however, is a materialist and does not believe in life after death. Indeed, even as he told me the story, he added by way of commentary, with a malicious smile, “It seems that the soul, after all, is a material entity too.” I disbelieve in ghosts almost as thoroughly as Chuck does. But I had felt an affection for Tock the poet, so I hurried straight to a bookshop and bought newspapers and magazines containing articles about Tock's ghost and photographs of it. Sure enough, when I examined the photographs, a kappa bearing some resemblance to Tock could be seen dimly materializing behind kappa of every age and sex. Yet what astonished me more than the photographs of Tock's ghost were the articles about it—especially the report issued by the Society for Psychical Research. I made a fairly literal translation of that report, so I shall give its general substance below. The remarks in parentheses, however, are annotations I added myself. —Report Concerning the Ghost of Mr. Tock, Poet. (Published in Issue 8,274 of the Journal of the Society for Psychical Research.) p.src: At 10:30 a.m. on September 17, we seventeen members, together with Mr. Peck, president of the Society for Psychical Research, assembled in a room of the said studio, accompanied by our most trusted medium, Mrs. Hop. The moment Mrs. Hop entered the said studio, she sensed a spiritual atmosphere; her entire body began to convulse, and she vomited several times. According to the lady, this was because the poet Mr. Tock had been so fond of strong tobacco that his spiritual atmosphere also contained nicotine. We members sat in silence around a round table with Mrs. Hop. After three minutes and twenty-five seconds, the lady fell with extraordinary suddenness into a somnambulistic state and became possessed by the spirit of the poet Mr. Tock. Proceeding in order of age, we members began the following exchange with the spirit of Mr. Tock possessing the lady. Question: Why do you appear as a ghost? Answer: To learn of my fame after death. Question: Do you—or spirits in general—still desire fame after death? Answer: I, at least, cannot help desiring it. Yet one Japanese poet I encountered held posthumous fame in contempt. Question: Do you know that poet's name? Answer: Regrettably, I have forgotten it. I remember only one of the seventeen-syllable poems he was fond of composing. Question: How does the poem go? Answer: “The old pond—a frog jumps in, the sound of water.” Question: Do you consider that poem a fine work? Answer: I do not necessarily consider it a bad one. But if “frog” were changed to “kappa,” it would be more splendidly brilliant still. Question: And what is the reason for that? Answer: Because we kappa feel an acute need to find kappa in every form of art. At this point, President Peck reminded us seventeen members that this was a special investigative meeting of the Society for Psychical Research, not a gathering for collective criticism. Question: What is life like for you spirits?

p.src: Answer: It is no different from your own lives. Question: Then do you regret having killed yourself? Answer: Not necessarily. If I grow weary of spiritual life, I shall take up a pistol again and return myself to life. Question: Is returning oneself to life easy or not? Tock's spirit answered this question with another question. To anyone who knew Tock, this must have seemed a perfectly natural exchange. Answer: Is killing oneself easy or not? Question: Are your lives eternal? Answer: As for our lives, theories abound and none can be trusted. Do not forget that, fortunately, we too have such religions as Christianity, Buddhism, Islam, and Zoroastrianism among us. Question: And what do you yourself believe? Answer: I have always been a skeptic. Question: Yet surely you do not at least doubt the existence of spirits? Answer: I cannot be as certain of it as you are. Question: How many friends do you have? Answer: My friendships extend through all ages and all countries, and must number no fewer than three hundred. Among the famous ones are Kleist, Mainländer, Weininger... Question: Are all your friends suicides? Answer: Not necessarily. Montaigne, who defended suicide, is one of my esteemed friends. I simply have no dealings with pessimists who did not kill themselves—with the likes of Schopenhauer. Question: Is Schopenhauer well? Answer: At present he is establishing a spiritual pessimism and debating whether it is proper to return oneself to life. Yet upon learning that cholera too was a bacterial disease, he appeared greatly relieved. We members then asked, one after another, for news of the spirits of Napoleon, Confucius, Dostoevsky, Darwin, Cleopatra, the Buddha, Demosthenes, Dante, Sen no Rikyū, and others. Unfortunately, Tock declined to answer in detail and instead asked us about various items of gossip concerning Tock himself.

p.src: Question: What is my posthumous reputation? Answer: One critic called you “one of the minor poets.” Question: He must be one of those who resented me for not sending him a copy of my poems. Have my complete works been published? Answer: Your complete works have been published, but they seem to be selling extremely poorly. Question: Three hundred years from now—when the copyright has expired—my complete works will surely be bought by everyone. What has become of the woman who lived with me? Answer: She has become the wife of Mr. Rack, the bookseller. Question: Unfortunately, she presumably still does not know that Rack's eye is artificial. What has become of my child? Answer: I hear the child is in the National Orphanage. After remaining silent for a while, Tock began asking questions again. Question: What has become of my house? Answer: It has become a certain photographer's studio. Question: What has become of my desk? Answer: No one knows what became of it. Question: In a drawer of my desk I left a bundle of letters I treasured—but fortunately that is none of the concern of you busy gentlemen. Now my spirit world is slowly sinking into twilight. I must take my leave of you. Farewell. Gentlemen. Farewell. My good gentlemen. With these final words, Mrs. Hop abruptly awakened once more. We seventeen members swear before God in heaven and vouch that this exchange truly occurred. (Furthermore, our trusted Mrs. Hop was paid at the daily rate she had received in her former days as an actress.)
